data.name: Quantum Chess
data.detailed_description:
Quantum Chess is the game from Caltech's "Anyone Can Quantum", where Paul Rudd beat Stephen Hawking. It is chess with new moves. A piece can split and stand on two squares at once. Two pieces can become entangled, so one outcome settles both. And when a capture depends on where a piece really is, the board measures. Almost every classical rule is still underneath: castling, en passant, promotion. There's no check or checkmate, you must capture the king, in all possible universes.

This is the Remaster, rebuilt from scratch. It is a free update for everyone who owns the original, and buying it on Steam adds six months of Premium to your account.

Owning Quantum Chess on Steam unlocks the exclusive Cloud Chamber theme. You can't get this anywhere else. The board sits inside a particle detector. Moves leave vapor trails, and when you measure, the branch that didn't happen breaks up into vapor. In the clip, a knight splits to d4 and g5, and its g5 half takes on f7. The board measures, the knight was on g5, and the d4 branch drifts away.

Cloud Chamber follows your Quantum Chess account to the web and your phone. Pick it in Settings, under Theme. It needs your own copy; a Family Sharing loan doesn't unlock it.

Select a piece, then drag between two squares it can reach. It now stands on both, half on each, and the ring around each half shows how much of it is there. Either half can move, threaten and block. Bring the halves back together with a merge.

A knight that is half on f3 takes on e5. Was it there to make the capture? The board measures and finds out. Plan for both answers, because your opponent will.

The queen slides to h5 through f3, where a split knight might be standing. If the knight is there, the queen didn't move. If it isn't, she went through. Until something measures, both stories are true, and one measurement settles the queen and the knight together.

The Alchemy League changes the rules every season. Season 1 runs from October 1 to January 1. It takes merges away and puts a phase dial beside the board. Turn the dial, split a piece back onto one of its own halves, and the two paths interfere: the dial decides where the piece ends up. In the clip, a rook split across a2 and a3 meets itself on a2 at 100%.

  • Free to play, on its own season ladder

  • Live games or correspondence

  • Practice with pass-and-play, no account needed

  • Rated games earn extra league badges, and participation can earn you the Alchemy board theme

The Quantum Lab is the sandbox: set up any position, play it out against the AI or yourself, undo and branch. Premium players can switch it to Universal QC, a ruleset with two more controls. The phase dial turns to any angle, not just quarter turns. The strength slider sets how a split divides a piece, so a knight can stand 79% on one square and 21% on the other, and a merge at the same strength undoes it. Premium also gets access to any Alchemy League season's rules, current or past, in the lab.

Ranked and casual games, cross-play with the browser version on one account.

  • Play a bot near your rating while the queue searches. When a real opponent turns up you get 15 seconds to join, and the bot game waits for you.

  • The open games board lists posted live and correspondence games. Post your own, or send a friend a private link.

  • A status pill on every screen shows what is waiting on you: a search, an open table, an opponent who sat down, or your move.

  • Notices reach you where you choose: in the app, by push, Discord message or Steam alert.

  • Correspondence give you days to make a move. You get a reminder before a deadline, and you can step back through any finished game.

  • Ask for a takeback in casual, ranked and league games.

  • Watch live games with the clocks running.

  • Tournaments: Swiss, round robin, knockout and arena, live or by correspondence. Anyone signed in can run one.

The tutorial teaches one move at a time on a live board. The in-app guides cover every rule, mode and overlay with boards you can play on. Then there are puzzles, AI opponents up to Aqaqaq, our quantum engine, and Steam achievements for the badges you earn.

For returning players

  • The Remaster is a free update in the same library entry.

  • Your copy unlocks Cloud Chamber and comes with six months of Premium. Link your Steam account on the account page and press Claim.

  • Ratings and stats started fresh, so the new ladder began with clean standings.

  • The original Unity version stays on the "legacy" beta branch: right-click Quantum Chess in your library, Properties, Betas.

If you reviewed the original, we'd love a second look.

Development happens in the open on our Discord. Come talk quantum chess, report bugs or test builds early.

data.short_description: The game where Paul Rudd beat Stephen Hawking. Chess where a piece can stand on two squares at once. Split, entangle and measure your way to checkmate. Owning it on Steam unlocks Cloud Chamber, a theme where every move leaves a vapor trail. The Remaster is free for owners of the original.

reviews.review:
Quantum Chess takes the familiar foundations of traditional chess and reshapes them around ideas inspired by quantum mechanics. Instead of simply introducing unusual pieces or alternative board layouts, it changes one of chess's most fundamental assumptions: that every piece occupies a definite position. Developed and published by Quantum Realm Games, the game uses concepts such as superposition and entanglement to create a strategy experience where uncertainty becomes just as important as calculation.

The centerpiece is the Quantum Move, which allows a piece to exist across multiple possible locations. This dramatically changes how players read the board. In ordinary chess, every threat and defensive position is visible and definite, allowing skilled players to calculate long sequences with confidence. Here, potential positions must also be considered. A piece that appears to threaten one part of the board may simultaneously influence another, forcing both players to evaluate possibilities rather than relying entirely on conventional chess patterns.

This mechanic gives the game its strongest quality: it makes experienced chess players reconsider habits they may have developed over many years. Familiar concepts such as development, board control, material advantage, king safety, and tactical exchanges remain useful, but they operate within a less predictable framework. Understanding standard chess therefore provides an advantage without automatically making someone proficient at this variation. Players must gradually learn how quantum states affect attacks, captures, and positional planning.

The unusual rules also give the experience an educational flavor. Quantum Chess was connected to Caltech IQIM's Anyone Can Quantum project, famously associated with a video featuring Paul Rudd and Stephen Hawking. The game does not attempt to function as a complete simulation of real quantum physics, but it does provide an entertaining way of encountering simplified ideas related to quantum phenomena. Superposition and entanglement become interactive concepts instead of merely scientific terminology, which gives the project an identity beyond being another chess variation.

Players can approach the experience through single-player play against the computer or compete against other people. Multiplayer is particularly well suited to the concept because both participants must deal with the same uncertainty and unconventional tactical possibilities. The game supports online PvP as well as shared or split-screen PvP and cross-platform multiplayer. Steam achievements, turn notifications, a level editor, Family Sharing, and other supporting features help make the package more substantial than a bare-bones experimental chess board.

Visually, the presentation is more functional than spectacular, but that approach works in its favor. A game built around complicated board states needs readability far more than elaborate visual effects. The interface keeps attention focused on pieces and their possible states, while the relatively lightweight technical requirements mean that powerful hardware is unnecessary. Windows, macOS, and Linux support further broaden its accessibility, and single-player functionality can be used offline.

The greatest obstacle is also the feature that makes the game distinctive. Traditional chess is attractive partly because there is no randomness hidden behind its moves. Every piece has a known location and every legal action has a predictable immediate result. Introducing quantum uncertainty disrupts that purity. Players who primarily enjoy chess for deterministic calculation may find the additional mechanics frustrating, while those who enjoy experimentation and adapting to uncertain situations are much more likely to appreciate the design.

There is also a noticeable learning curve. Someone unfamiliar with chess already has an entire set of movement rules and strategic principles to understand, while an experienced player must learn how those established principles interact with quantum mechanics. Early matches can consequently feel confusing. Once the underlying rules become familiar, however, the apparent chaos begins to reveal a different kind of strategic depth. Decisions become exercises in managing probabilities and potential board states rather than simply finding a single optimal continuation.

Steam Deck compatibility is currently listed as Unknown rather than officially Verified or Playable. The game does have Linux support and modest hardware requirements, which may provide encouraging conditions for handheld use, but those factors should not be interpreted as an official Steam Deck compatibility rating. Players specifically purchasing it for Steam Deck should therefore regard handheld compatibility as unverified.

Quantum Chess is ultimately more interesting as an experimental strategy game than as a replacement for conventional chess. Its greatest accomplishment is taking an extremely familiar board game and making players uncertain about assumptions that normally seem absolute. It will not appeal equally to chess purists, particularly anyone who dislikes probability influencing carefully constructed plans, but its unusual mechanics create an intellectual challenge rarely found in conventional digital board games. As a combination of chess, scientific inspiration, and strategic experimentation, it provides a genuinely distinctive experience.

Rating: 7/10
